messages.author: ee65f9feb643484e
messages.subject: Calculation of residuals when missing="fiml"
parts:
Dear lavaan group,

I understand how the residuals are calculated if listwise deletion is used, but I don't understand how the residuals are calculated if FIML is used.

Example:

######################################################################################

set.seed(1)

n <- 100

d <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n),
                x2 = rnorm(n),
                x3 = rnorm(n),
                x4 = rnorm(n))

d[1:20, "x1"] <- NA
d[1:10, "x2"] <- NA

mod <- 'F =~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4'

sem1 <- sem(model = mod, data=d, std.lv=TRUE, likelihood="wishart")
sem2 <- sem(model = mod, data=d, std.lv=TRUE, likelihood="wishart", missing="fiml")

resid(sem1)$cov[1:4, 1:4]
(cov(d, use="complete.obs") - fitted(sem1)$cov)[1:4, 1:4]  ## these are the same

resid(sem2)$cov[1:4, 1:4]
(cov(d, use="pair") - fitted(sem2)$cov)[1:4, 1:4]  ## these are not the same

# Note that  inspect(sem2, "sampstat")$cov[1:4, 1:4]   is the same as  cov(d, use="pair")

#########################################################################################

I'd really appreciate it if someone could explain how resid(sem2)$cov is calculated.

Thanks,
Mark

messages.subject: Re: Calculation of residuals when missing="fiml"
parts:
I now see that the residuals are 

(sem2@Sam...@missing.h1[[1]]$sigma - fitted(sem2)$cov)[1:4, 1:4]

but I don't understand the reason for modifying the observed covariance matrix.

Could someone please explain that?

Thanks,
Mark

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: Calculation of residuals when missing="fiml"
parts:
On 01/16/2014 04:55 AM, Mark Seeto wrote:
> I now see that the residuals are
>
> (sem2@Sam...@missing.h1[[1]]$sigma - fitted(sem2)$cov)[1:4, 1:4]
>
> but I don't understand the reason for modifying the observed covariance
> matrix.

When data is missing, there is no (unique) observed covariance matrix.
But we can estimate it, using maximum likelihood (and without losing any
data). This is where the EM algorithm comes in. The result is an
estimated covariance matrix that is indeed stored in
@Sampl...@missing.h1[[1]]$sigma, and it is this one that is used to
compute the covariance-based residuals.

Yves.
